source.title: Steering Without Breaking: Mechanistically Informed Interventions for Discrete Diffusion Language Models
source.authors: Han-Han Zhou; Shamik Roy; Rashmi Gangadharaiah

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies SAE-based feature analysis to discrete diffusion language models and reports results on recovered semantic features and their stability across denoising noise levels. It does not reproduce the toy-model superposition setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports SAE feature recovery and feature-stability results used below. Layer-probing results used to select layers, steering results that only evaluate the proposed steering method, and cross-attribute interference results are not evidence about feature capacity or polysemanticity as stated in the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses TopK SAEs on four discrete diffusion LMs as a tool to pick attribute features and design adaptive steering schedules. Its main results are about its own steering method. Its SAE analyses (top-3 vocabulary projections, Cohen's d spread, noise-bin stability, cross-model alignment) do not test superposition, capacity, neuron polysemanticity, or whether SAE features are complete or canonical units. Feature recovery is assumed, not evaluated: there are no reconstruction or interpretability-rate measures against a baseline.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but misweighted. The authors conclude that SAE features show attributes committing during DLM denoising at different steps, with different sharpness and effect sizes. They conclude that an adaptive schedule concentrating intervention where each attribute is forming improves the control–quality trade-off over uniform and interval-restricted steering. The noise-level robustness of feature discriminability is an appendix finding, not a main conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: Uses TopK SAEs, contrastive attribute selection, temporal activation analysis, and feature-based steering on discrete diffusion language models; it does not use the original toy-network superposition setup or measure superposition capacity.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature discriminability varies across noise bins, layers, attributes, and models. The paper reports that effective dimensionality differs between MDLM and SEDD despite their shared architecture and data.

fits_no_version.finding: SEDD spreads sentiment and formality attribute signal across 2.6x and 2.2x more SAE features (effective dimensionality) than MDLM, which has the same architecture and data but a different loss. Topic is more concentrated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training objective shapes how distributed attribute signal is across SAE dictionary features.

fits_no_version.finding: For MDLM, the discriminability (Cohen's |d|) of top-20 SAE features varies moderately across diffusion noise bins: median CV 14–22%, with 65–90% of features below 25% CV.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features trained on mixed-noise activations keep their attribute discriminability across denoising noise levels.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features from MDLM and SEDD are near-orthogonal (mean best-match cosine ~0.08). Same-loss-family pairs align more (MDLM–DREAM 0.23 mean, 0.54 max; MDLM–LLaDA 0.15 mean, 0.47 max) (Fig 3d, Table 36).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-model universality of SAE features depends on the training objective more than on architecture.

record.problems: Evidence for feature recovery covers four discrete diffusion models and selected attributes, not autoregressive LLMs or a comprehensive inventory of model representations. The stability analysis across noise bins is reported for MDLM only and measures discriminability rather than completeness or canonicality. Feature interpretation relies partly on vocabulary projections and off-the-shelf classifiers.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results were omitted.

untested.parts: No toy models, no sparsity-dependent transition, no feature geometry under compression.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity-allocation analysis.
No analysis of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
No measure of features spread across neurons. SAE recovery is assumed: no reconstruction quality, interpretability rate, or baseline comparison is reported.
No test of completeness, seed or size stability, or canonicality of SAE features within a model.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The record treats SAE-based steering and interpretability results as tests of V4/V5. They are tool use (T4). The study never tests whether the models' representations are superposed or whether SAEs are the right decomposition. Appendix C.3 also claims feature activations vary under 15% across noise levels, but Table 17 shows median CV of 14–22%. Cross-model alignment (Table 36) has no row; it is recorded under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, feature overlap or near-orthogonal geometry under superposition, or sparsity-dependent transitions.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity arises from competition for limited representational capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
Tests SAE recovery of selected semantic attributes in four discrete diffusion language models. Does not test autoregressive LLMs or measure how features are distributed across ordinary neurons.
Tests variation in feature discriminability across noise levels for MDLM. Does not establish completeness of the SAE dictionary or whether features are canonical units within a model.
Uses SAE decoder columns as directions but does not compare one-dimensional features against multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: MDLM-124M
rows.operation_detail: Selected contrastive SAE features for sentiment, topic, and style, then projected decoder columns through the unembedding matrix for vocabulary grounding.

conditions.value: positive sentiment, sports topic, formal style

rows.measure: Semantic coherence of SAE-recovered attribute features via top-token projections
rows.value: The authors state that vocabulary grounding confirms retained features are semantically coherent; Table 8 shows top-token projections for the top 3 positive-d and negative-d features per attribute at layer 7.
rows.note: The feature extraction retains top 50 features per direction per layer that pass the stated statistical test; top 20 per direction are used for steering.
rows.check: Qualitative top-3 vocabulary projections for hand-selected contrastive features. Many listed tokens are incoherent (e.g. 'dyl, anooga, rongh'). This uses SAE features as a tool and does not measure whether the model holds sparse features in superposition. No baseline.

rows.subject: SEDD-124M
rows.operation_detail: Compared effective dimensionality of contrastive SAE feature signal with MDLM at layer 7.

conditions.value: same architecture and data, different diffusion loss; MDLM reference

rows.measure: Effective dimensionality of feature effect-size distribution
rows.value: SEDD spreads sentiment across 2.6× more features than MDLM.
rows.note: The paper defines effective dimensionality as (sum d)^2 / sum d^2.
rows.check: Effective dimensionality is computed over SAE-feature Cohen's d values, not over neurons. It compares two models' attribute spread across dictionary features and does not show features spread across neurons or superposition.

rows.subject: SEDD-124M

rows.measure: Effective dimensionality of feature effect-size distribution
rows.value: Topic signal is comparable between SEDD and MDLM (0.8× total effect size); the paper says topic is more concentrated than the other attributes.

rows.check: Same construct issue as R5. Figure 3c also appears to show 0.8x for topic effective dimensionality, not only total effect size. 'Partial' is not a meaningful state for a between-model comparison.

rows.subject: MDLM-124M
rows.operation_detail: Measured variation in feature Cohen's d across five noise-level bins.
rows.measure: Coefficient of variation of |d| across noise bins for top-20 features
rows.value: Median CV 19.8%; mean CV 24.6%; 25% of features have CV < 15% and 65% have CV < 25%.
rows.note: This measures noise-level stability of discriminability, not completeness or canonicality.
rows.check: CV of feature discriminability across noise bins is stability over diffusion noise level, not stability of SAE features across seeds or dictionary sizes, completeness, or canonicality as V5 names.
